content: Efforts will be made to prepare for the patient’s death, if deemed appropriate. Every effort will be taken to ensure that the patient receives care in the location of their choice. If the patient wishes to remain at home, support will be provided to assist family caregivers with home care, as necessary. Decisions regarding the goals of care will be made collaboratively between the healthcare team and the patient and/or their family caregivers, as appropriate. Bereavement support will also be made available. Palliative care services can be initiated in various ways, as there is no universally optimal starting point for all settings. The options presented in this manual are intended to be considered and discussed within the national context. Some approaches may complement each other and can be implemented simultaneously, depending on the available resources and context. It is essential to evaluate which services are already providing palliative care, including those in the non-governmental sector, and to build upon these existing resources. This section outlines different models and strategies for establishing palliative care services, with a focus on integrating palliative care into existing healthcare systems. The service delivery model must consider the country’s social and healthcare system context. All examples provided in this guide will require further adaptation to meet local needs. Palliative care services can be established or expanded in several ways, depending on the local situation. For example, a country may choose to begin by: 1. Establishing a palliative home-care service or integrating palliative home care into existing home-care services. 2. Setting up palliative care in a community setting. 3. Integrating palliative care services into a district or general hospital. 4. Creating a palliative care service specifically for children, including neonates. 5. Establishing a standalone palliative care center or hospice. 6. Taking an integrated approach at the district level. It is important to note that palliative care services at different levels all serve a critical function as part of a comprehensive palliative care system. Patients requiring palliative care may need support from various levels of palliative care services throughout their care journey. Therefore, referral pathways must be in place to ensure seamless transitions for patients and their families. Home-based palliative care provides care to individuals with chronic, life-limiting health conditions, such as cancer, advanced cardiac, renal, and respiratory diseases, HIV/AIDS, and chronic neurological disorders, in the comfort of their own homes. This type of care is best delivered by a multidisciplinary team trained in palliative care, including doctors, nurses, community health workers, and volunteers. Home-based palliative care offers several advantages. Many patients feel more comfortable in their homes than in healthcare settings. This approach integrates family members into the care process, ensuring that patients have easy access to care. It also provides advice and support to family members to help them in their caregiving roles. The home-care team can facilitate referrals to additional services as needed. Home-based care helps patients and families maintain privacy and confidentiality while increasing community awareness of palliative care. Local resources and support networks can be mobilized, and community health workers can provide training to others in the area. A basic home-based palliative care service can be established relatively simply. Essential requirements include a safe home environment for the care team to visit, a secure and accessible place to store medicines and equipment, and transportation for the team to visit patients’ homes. Team members also need mobile phones to stay in contact with patients and families around the clock. Patients and their caregivers should be able to contact the home-care team outside of scheduled visits. At a minimum, a full-time nurse and a part-time doctor are required for a home-care team, although this depends on the country’s regulatory and healthcare system norms. Ideally, the team should include nurses, doctors, psychologists/counselors, social workers, and trained volunteers or community health workers. Training for the team should include both theoretical and hands-on components. Family caregivers should also receive training, with simple printed information on managing patient care at home. Standard forms should be used for documenting patient records, and patients/families should ideally sign a consent form. A health record should be maintained for each patient, and records of all medicine usage, especially morphine, should comply with local laws and regulations. Community-based palliative care services are those offered at a community health center (CHC) or run with community participation. Community participation involves the active involvement of people in a community to address their own problems, including needs assessment, planning, implementation, resource mobilization, day-to-day management, and program evaluation. In resource-limited settings, community-based palliative care services can achieve significant coverage for patients with chronic, life-limiting health conditions. These services should ideally be initiated in collaboration with local health authorities and follow the planning processes used in the health system. Community-based approaches can also be implemented by community organizations that wish to establish palliative care services for their community, which can later be integrated into the health system. These services are typically provided by both healthcare professionals and community health workers/volunteers. At a minimum, paid doctors and nurses are required, who may work at the CHC and support community health workers or volunteers visiting patients and families at home. Healthcare professionals based at a CHC can also visit patients at home when needed and maintain contact with patients and families via mobile phones. The team may include other voluntary allied health professionals if available. Community health workers or volunteers, supported by healthcare professionals, will provide basic home care.
